proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(m\in\mathcal M_n(B)\) and \(l\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\), \(\overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}=r_l^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_l}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\) is a finite sum of coordinates of \(D=(Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\), and therefore is \(D\)-measurable.  If \(A_l=1\), then \(Z_j=1\) for all \(j\in B_l\); \(\mathrm{ass{:}block\text{-}exposure}\) gives \(e_i(Z)=a\) for every \(i\in B_l\).  Consistency in the definition of \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\) then gives
\[
 \overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}={1\over r_l}\sum_{i\in B_l}Y_i(a)=\mu_l(a)
\]
by \(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}means}\).  The identical argument with \(C_l=1\), all assignments zero, and exposure \(b\) gives \(\overline Y_l^{\mathrm{obs}}=\mu_l(b)\).  Nonemptiness of \(B_l\) in \(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\) ensures \(r_l>0\), so both displayed averages are defined.  Fixedness in \(\mathrm{ass{:}fixed\text{-}schedule}\) ensures that the right sides are nonrandom design quantities, and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcomes}\) puts all the averages in \([-1/2,1/2]\).

Disjointness in \(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\) and the product assignment law \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\) make the subvectors \(Z_{B_l}\) independent.  There are \(2^{r_l}\) equiprobable assignments in block \(l\), exactly one all treated and exactly one all controlled.  Hence
\[
 P_Z(A_l=1)=P_Z(C_l=1)=2^{-r_l}=q_l,\qquad
 P_Z(H_l=1)=1-2q_l,\qquad A_lC_l=0.
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\), on the only events on which it is multiplied by a nonzero indicator,
\[
 X_l={w_l\over q_l}\{A_l\mu_l(a)-C_l\mu_l(b)\}.
\]
Thus, using the categorical probabilities,
\[
 \mathbb E_ZX_l=w_l\{\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\},\qquad
 \mathbb E_ZX_l^2={w_l^2\over q_l}\{\mu_l(a)^2+\mu_l(b)^2\}.
\]
The support condition \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcomes}\) gives \(|\mu_l(a)|,|\mu_l(b)|\le1/2\); therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_Z(X_l)\le\mathbb E_ZX_l^2\le{w_l^2\over2q_l},\qquad
 \sum_l\operatorname{Var}_Z(X_l)\le {S\over2}.
\]
For the increment bound, the three possible values of \(X_l\) are \((w_l/q_l)\mu_l(a)\), \(-(w_l/q_l)\mu_l(b)\), and zero.  Each belongs to \([-w_l/(2q_l),w_l/(2q_l)]\), and its expectation is a convex combination of these three values.  Hence its distance from any support point is at most the support diameter \(w_l/q_l\), which is at most \(M\).  Independence of \(X_l\) follows from independence of the block assignments and fixedness of the schedule.

Measurability follows from \(\mathrm{def{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\), \(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}ht}\), and \(\mathrm{def{:}clipped\text{-}ht}\).  Summing the expectation identity in \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\) and using the definition of \(\theta\) gives \(\mathbb E_Z\widehat\theta=\theta\).

We use a slightly sharper support calculation than the diameter bound stated in that lemma.  Put \(c_l=w_l/q_l\), \(u_l=c_l\mu_l(a)\), and \(v_l=-c_l\mu_l(b)\).  Then \(|u_l|,|v_l|\le c_l/2\) and \(X_l\) has values \(u_l,v_l,0\) with probabilities \(q_l,q_l,1-2q_l\).  For a realized value \(u_l\),
\[
 |u_l-\mathbb EX_l|=|(1-q_l)u_l-q_lv_l|
 \le(1-q_l){c_l\over2}+q_l{c_l\over2}={c_l\over2};
\]
the same holds for \(v_l\), while \(|0-\mathbb EX_l|=q_l|u_l+v_l|\le q_lc_l\le c_l/2\).  Thus \(|X_l-\mathbb EX_l|\le M/2\), and \(v:=\sum_l\operatorname{Var}(X_l)\le S/2\) by \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\).

For a centered variable \(W\) with \(|W|\le b\), expansion of the exponential and \(|W|^k\le b^{k-2}W^2\) for \(k\ge2\) give
\[
 \log\mathbb E e^{zW}\le {z^2\mathbb EW^2\over2(1-bz/3)},\qquad 0\le z<3/b.
\]
Multiplying these moment-generating-function bounds for the independent centered summands, and using exponential Markov with \(b=M/2\), gives
\[
 P_Z\{\widehat\theta-\theta\ge y\}
 \le\exp\{-y^2/(2v+2by/3)\},
\]
and the same inequality holds for the lower tail.  The elementary Bernstein inversion, obtained by substituting \(y=\sqrt{2vx}+2bx/3\) in the preceding exponent, yields
\[
 P_Z\left\{|\widehat\theta-\theta|>
 \sqrt{2v\log(2/\alpha)}+{2b\over3}\log(2/\alpha)\right\}\le\alpha.
\]
Using \(2v\le S\) and \(2b\le M\) makes the displayed radius no larger than \(h_\alpha\).  Since \(\theta\in[-1,1]\) by the outcome support and \(\sum_lw_l=1\), clipping the interval to \([-1,1]\) cannot remove \(\theta\) on the concentration event.  Finally, the intersection of two intervals has length at most the smaller of their lengths, so
\[
 \operatorname{len}(I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha})
 \le\min\{2,2h_\alpha\}=2\min\{1,h_\alpha\}.
\]
As an exact small-instance check, take \(n=3\), block sizes \((1,2)\), hence
\((w_1,w_2)=(1/3,2/3)\) and \((q_1,q_2)=(1/2,1/4)\).  Put
\((\mu_1(a),\mu_1(b))=(1/2,-1/2)\) and
\((\mu_2(a),\mu_2(b))=(-1/2,1/2)\).  Enumeration of all
\(2^3\) assignments gives \(X_1=1/3\) always, while \(X_2=-4/3\)
on either unanimous assignment of the second block and \(X_2=0\) on
either mixed assignment.  Thus
\[
 P_Z(\widehat\theta=-1)=P_Z(\widehat\theta=1/3)=1/2,\qquad
 \mathbb E_Z\widehat\theta=-1/3=\theta,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\theta)=4/9\le S/2=1.
\]
This exhaustive check verifies mutual exclusion, both inverse-probability
factors, and clipping in the smallest unequal-block example.

For fixed \(v\), the schedule in \(\mathrm{def{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\) is nonrandom, all its values are either \(v_l\in\{-1/2,1/2\}\) or zero, and it uses the partition and exposure map required by \(\mathrm{def{:}model\text{-}class}\).  Thus the five defining assumptions of that class hold.  Direct substitution in \(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}means}\) gives
\[
 \mu_l^v(a)=v_l,\qquad \mu_l^v(b)=0,\qquad
 \theta(m_v)=\sum_lw_lv_l=T(v).
\]
Under the balanced product design, \(K_l=A_l=\mathbf1\{Z_{B_l}=\mathbf1_{B_l}\}\) are independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities \(q_l=2^{-r_l}\).  The exposure definition and the schedule give \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=K_lv_l\) for \(i\in B_l\), so \(O_l=(K_l,K_lv_l)\) is measurable from \(D\).

Conditional on \(K_l=1\), the block assignment is the point mass at \(\mathbf1_{B_l}\).  Conditional on \(K_l=0\), each of the other \(2^{r_l}-1\) assignments retains its common unconditional mass \(2^{-r_l}\), hence is uniform.  Block independence is preserved by coordinatewise conditioning, proving
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(Z\mid K=k)=\bigotimes_l\nu_{l,k_l}.                     \tag{17}
\]
Because these are finite distributions, each \(F_l\) can be chosen as the inverse distribution function after any fixed enumeration of \(\{0,1\}^{B_l}\); it is measurable.  The measure-preserving property of \(\beta\) makes \((R_0,R_1,\ldots,R_L)\) independent uniforms.  Equations (17) and the definition of \(Y^*\) therefore imply, for every fixed \(v\),
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(D^*,R_0\mid V=v)=\operatorname{Law}_{Z,R_0,m_v}(D,R_0).
\]
Composing the measurable maps proves measurability of \(\Lambda_\Gamma\).  Applying the last equality of laws to the indicators of coverage and to the nonnegative measurable length functional gives the two displayed equalities in the claim.

If \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\), pointwise honesty applied to each legal \(m_v\) gives coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(v\).  Averaging that inequality over \(V\sim\pi_t\) gives the asserted \(Q_t\)-coverage.  Likewise, for every \(t\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_\Gamma)
 =\sum_v\pi_t(v)\mathbb E_{K,R}[\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_\Gamma)\mid V=v]
 \le\sup_v\mathbb E_{K,R}[\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_\Gamma)\mid V=v],
\]
and the latter supremum is bounded by the supremum over all \(m'\in\mathcal M_n(B)\), because every \(m_v\) lies in that class.  This proves every transfer claim without discarding the all-control or mixed assignment ancillary and without assuming a posterior-spread inequality.

Let \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\).  Since
\[
 \|s\|_\infty={M\over\sqrt S},
\]
the displayed no-dominance hypothesis with the constant from \(\mathrm{thm{:}weighted\text{-}erasure\text{-}spread}\) verifies its premise.  For any \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\), \(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\) constructs \(\Lambda_\Gamma\), supplies the required \(Q_t\)-coverage, and bounds the original worst-case expected length below by every \(Q_t\)-average length.  The weighted-erasure theorem therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{m\in\mathcal M_n(B)}\mathbb E_m\operatorname{len}(\Gamma)
 \ge c_1\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\}.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\Gamma\) proves the lower bound, including externally randomized procedures.

For the upper bound, \(S=\sum_lw_l(w_l/q_l)\le M\sum_lw_l=M\).  Hence the no-dominance condition implies \(\sqrt{Sx}\le c_0\).  Also \(x\le\log(2/\alpha)\le(3/2)x\) for \(\alpha\le1/4\).  Thus
\[
 h_\alpha\le\sqrt{3/2}\sqrt{Sx}+{1\over2}M x
 \le\left(\sqrt{3/2}+{c_0\over2}\right)\sqrt{Sx}.
\]
The interval of \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\) belongs to \(\mathfrak C_\alpha\) and has length at most \(2\min\{1,h_\alpha\}\).  Taking, for example, \(C_1=4\) after decreasing \(c_0\le1\) proves the upper bound.

For a fixed subset \(J\), define the observed statistic \(\widehat\theta_J=\sum_{l\in J}X_l(D)\), the retained target \(\theta_J=\sum_{l\in J}w_l\{\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\}\), and \(b_J=\sum_{l\notin J}w_l\).  Outcome boundedness gives \(|\theta-\theta_J|\le b_J\).  Repeating the proof of \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\) on \(J\) gives, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\),
\[
 |\widehat\theta_J-\theta_J|\le
 h_J:=\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)\sum_{l\in J}{w_l^2\over q_l}}
 +{\log(2/\alpha)\over3}\max_{l\in J}{w_l\over q_l}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 I_J=[-1,1]\cap[\widehat\theta_J-b_J-h_J,\widehat\theta_J+b_J+h_J]
\]
is \(D\)-measurable, covers \(\theta\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), and has length at most \(2\min\{1,b_J+h_J\}\).  There are finitely many subsets, so choose a deterministic minimizer \(J^*\), breaking ties lexicographically.  By \(\mathrm{def{:}trimmed\text{-}radius}\), \(b_{J^*}+h_{J^*}=\rho_\alpha(w,q)\).  Hence \(I_{J^*}\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\) and has the claimed length.  For \(J=\varnothing\), the statistic and maximum are zero, exactly as stipulated in the definition.

For a size-one block, \((w_l,q_l)=(1/12,1/2)\), so \(q_l/w_l=6\); for a size-three block, \((w_l,q_l)=(1/4,1/8)\), so \(q_l/w_l=1/2\).  If the three size-three coordinates cap and the other three do not, the active constraint is
\[
 {3\over8}+3\cdot{1\over2}\left({\lambda_\alpha\over6}\right)^2
 ={3\over8}+{\lambda_\alpha^2\over24}=\log4.
\]
Thus \(\lambda_\alpha=\sqrt{24(\log4-3/8)}\).  Numerically \(1/2<\lambda_\alpha<6\), verifying the proposed cap pattern against both breakpoints.  The objective at this certified optimizer is
\[
 3\cdot{1\over4}+3\cdot{1\over12}{\lambda_\alpha\over6}
 ={3\over4}+\sqrt{{\log4-3/8\over24}}\approx0.9553.
\]
For \(\rho_0\), retain the three size-one blocks and omit the other three.  The corresponding value is
\[
 {3\over4}+\sqrt{3{(1/12)^2\over1/2}}={3\over4}+{1\over\sqrt{24}}\approx0.9541,
\]
which proves the stated upper certificate.

For \(b>0\), abbreviate
\[
 \Omega_b=\max\left\{\sum_lw_l\delta_l:0\le\delta_l\le1, \sum_lq_l\delta_l^2\le b\right\},
 \quad
 R_b=\inf_J\left\{\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+\sqrt{b\sum_{l\in J}w_l^2/q_l}\right\}.
\]
The Cauchy--Schwarz argument in \(\mathrm{thm{:}water\text{-}filling\text{-}partial\text{-}frontier}\) gives \(\Omega_b\le R_b\).  Repeating (18)--(19) without the Bernstein maximum term gives \(R_b\le4\Omega_b\).  In particular,
\[
 \Omega_1\le\rho_0\le4\Omega_1.                                            \tag{20}
\]
For fixed \(\alpha\), \(x=x_\alpha\ge1\), \(\omega_\alpha=\Omega_x\), and scaling a feasible vector shows
\[
 \Omega_1\le\Omega_x\le\sqrt x\,\Omega_1.                                \tag{21}
\]
Indeed \(\delta/\sqrt x\) is feasible for \(\Omega_1\) whenever \(\delta\) is feasible for \(\Omega_x\).  Equations (20)--(21) prove \(\omega_\alpha\to0\) if and only if \(\rho_0\to0\).

The fixed-level lower bound and universal upper bound in the partial water-filling theorem give
\[
 c_\alpha\omega_\alpha\le\mathcal R_\alpha\le8\omega_\alpha.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\) if and only if \(\omega_\alpha\to0\), completing the three-way equivalence.

Choosing \(J=\{1,\ldots,L\}\) in \(\rho_0\) gives \(\rho_0\le\sqrt S\), so \(S\to0\) is sufficient.  It is not necessary: let \(n_k=2^k\), take one block of size \(2k\), and partition the remaining \(n_k-2k\) units into singleton blocks.  The large block has \(w=2k/2^k\), \(q=2^{-2k}\), and contributes \(4k^2\) to \(S\), so \(S\to\infty\).  Omitting it in \(\rho_0\) gives
\[
 \rho_0\le {2k\over2^k}+\sqrt{{2(n_k-2k)\over n_k^2}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This legal triangular array proves the final assertion.

There are \(k\) blocks of each size, so \(n=2k+4k=6k\).  Balanced Bernoulli assignment gives \(q=2^{-r}\); hence the size-two stratum has \((w,q)=(2/(6k),1/4)=(1/(3k),1/4)\), and the size-four stratum has \((w,q)=(4/(6k),1/16)=(2/(3k),1/16)\).  Therefore
\[
 S=k{(1/(3k))^2\over1/4}+k{(2/(3k))^2\over1/16}
 ={4\over9k}+{64\over9k}={68\over9k},
\]
and
\[
 M=\max\left\{{4\over3k},{32\over3k}\right\}={32\over3k}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 {M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\over\sqrt S}
 ={32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\over\sqrt{68k}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For sufficiently large \(k\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}frontier}\) applies and gives the asserted order \(\sqrt{68\log(1/\alpha)/(9k)}\).  A common block size would force one common value \(2^{-r}\) and one common breakpoint \(q/w=n2^{-r}/r\); it cannot equal both \(1/4\) and \(1/16\), nor the two resulting breakpoints.

If every block has size \(r\), the partition identity gives \(Lr=n\), hence \(L=n/r\).  Directly from the definitions,
\[
 q_l=2^{-r},\qquad w_l={r\over n},
\]
and therefore
\[
 S={n\over r}{(r/n)^2\over2^{-r}}={r2^r\over n},\qquad
 M={(r/n)\over2^{-r}}={r2^r\over n}=S.
\]
The no-dominance premise is \(S\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\le c_0\sqrt S\), equivalently \(S\log(1/\alpha)\le c_0^2\).  The frontier theorem then gives length order \(\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}=\sqrt{r2^r\log(1/\alpha)/n}\) throughout \(0<\alpha\le1/4\); no additional confidence cutoff is used.

On a valid disjoint union of cliques, \(N_G[i]=B_l\) for \(i\in B_l\).  Hence the first package column and the reference all-treated column are both \(A_l\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}package\text{-}label\text{-}maps}\), the second package column is \(1-A_l\), whereas the reference all-control column is \(C_l\).  Since \(A_lC_l=0\) by \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\),
\[
 1-A_l=C_l\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_l+C_l=1.
\]
Coordinatewise equality of the two matrices is therefore equivalent to this identity in every block.  A mixed block has \((A_l,C_l)=(0,0)\), so its package second column is one and its reference second column is zero, giving the promised explicit witness.

The remaining conclusions now follow by executing the checks in \(\mathrm{def{:}software\text{-}diagnostic}\) in their stated order.  On a valid graph, equality of both supplied matrices with their independently specified maps is checked before their mutual equality.  If all checks pass, \(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\) makes the reported block means observable, the balanced design gives \(q_l=2^{-r_l}\), and the definitions compute \(w_l,S,M,\omega_\alpha,\rho_\alpha\), and \(I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}\) exactly.  The finite and trimmed upper theorems certify the reported intervals.  If equality fails, the finite matrix domain supplies a first unequal coordinate and the definition suppresses interval output.  Finally, if some \(N_G[i]\ne B_l\), the graph check fails before either label comparison; the unequal finite sets provide a crossing-neighborhood or missing-clique-edge witness, and again the definition suppresses interval output.  These branches are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

theorem.statement:
There exist universal \(c_0,c_1,c_2\in(0,1)\) such that, for every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and every \((w,q)\) with \(\sum_lq_ls_l^2=1\) and \(\|s\|_\infty\sqrt{x_\alpha}\le c_0\), one has \([-c_2\sqrt{x_\alpha},c_2\sqrt{x_\alpha}]\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}}\), and every measurable, possibly externally randomized interval \(\Lambda(O,R)\) obeys
\[
\inf_{|t|\le c_2\sqrt{x_\alpha}}Q_t\{T(V)\in\Lambda(O,R)\}\ge1-\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sup_{|t|\le c_2\sqrt{x_\alpha}}\mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
\ge c_1\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx_\alpha}\}.
\]
theorem.proof_tex:
By \(s_l=w_l/(q_l\sqrt S)\),
\[
 \sum_lq_ls_l^2={1\over S}\sum_l{w_l^2\over q_l}=1.
\]
Choose \(c_0=c_{\mathrm e}\), \(c_2=c_{\mathrm p}\), and \(c_1=c_{\mathrm s}\) from \(\mathrm{lem{:}product\text{-}erasure\text{-}interval\text{-}calculus}\).  Since \(c_0c_2\le1\), \(|t|\|s\|_\infty\le1\) whenever \(|t|\le c_2\sqrt{x_\alpha}\); hence this interval is contained in \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}}\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}tilted\text{-}sign\text{-}prior}\).  The implication is exactly the first conclusion of the cited proved calculus lemma, under the joint laws in \(\mathrm{def{:}weighted\text{-}erasure\text{-}law}\).  Its last conditioning step includes the independent \(R\), so no restriction to deterministic intervals is made.

theorem.statement:
Let \(x_\alpha=\log(1/\alpha)\) and \(x_{2,\alpha}=\log(2/\alpha)\).  The optimizer in \(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) is correct and is certified by the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker equations: if \(x_\alpha\ge\sum_lq_l\), then \(\delta_l^*=1\); otherwise there is a unique \(\lambda_\alpha>0\) with
\[
 \sum_lq_l\min\{1,\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l\}^2=x_\alpha,\qquad
 \delta_l^*=\min\{1,\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l\}.
\]
For every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\rho_\alpha(w,q)\le4\omega_\alpha(w,q),
 \qquad \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\le8\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\]
For each fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), there is a constant \(c_\alpha>0\), depending only on \(\alpha\), such that
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\ge c_\alpha\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\]
Thus the asserted global equivalence is proved at every fixed confidence level, while this result does not assert that the lower constant is uniform as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).  If no coordinate caps, equivalently \(M\sqrt{x_\alpha}\le\sqrt S\), then \(\omega_\alpha(w,q)=\sqrt{Sx_\alpha}\).
theorem.proof_tex:
The feasible set is compact and the objective continuous, so a maximizer exists.  If \(x_\alpha\ge\sum_lq_l\), the coordinatewise largest feasible vector is \((1,\ldots,1)\).  Otherwise the quadratic constraint is active.  With multiplier \(\eta>0\), stationarity on an uncapped coordinate gives \(w_l-2\eta q_l\delta_l=0\), whereas complementary slackness gives the cap when this value exceeds one.  Thus \(\delta_l=\min\{1,\lambda w_l/q_l\}\), where \(\lambda=(2\eta)^{-1}\).  The left side of the constraint equation is continuous and strictly increasing from zero to \(\sum_lq_l\), up to the last breakpoint, proving existence and uniqueness of \(\lambda\).  The objective is linear and the constraint set convex; the KKT inequality
\[
 \sum_lw_l(\delta_l-\delta_l^*)
 \le {1\over2\lambda}\sum_lq_l\{\delta_l^2-(\delta_l^*)^2\}\le0
\]
after adding the nonnegative cap multipliers certifies global optimality.

For any feasible \(\delta\) and any \(J\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \sum_lw_l\delta_l
 \le\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+\sqrt{x_\alpha\sum_{l\in J}w_l^2/q_l}
 \le\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+\sqrt{x_{2,\alpha}\sum_{l\in J}w_l^2/q_l}
 +{x_{2,\alpha}\over3}\max_{l\in J}{w_l\over q_l}.
\]
Maximizing and then minimizing proves \(\omega_\alpha\le\rho_\alpha\).

If all coordinates cap, both sides equal one by taking \(J=\varnothing\).  Otherwise use the certified optimizer and put \(J=\{l:\delta_l^*<1/2\}\), \(D=J^c\).  Then
\[
 \sum_{l\in D}w_l\le2\omega_\alpha,\qquad
 S_J\le{x_\alpha\over\lambda_\alpha^2},\qquad
 M_J\le{1\over2\lambda_\alpha}.                                            \tag{18}
\]
Moreover, separating capped and uncapped coordinates in the active constraint gives
\[
 {x_\alpha\over\lambda_\alpha}
 =\sum_l{q_l(\delta_l^*)^2\over\lambda_\alpha}
 \le\sum_lw_l\delta_l^*=\omega_\alpha.                                    \tag{19}
\]
Indeed equality holds for an uncapped coordinate, and for a capped one \(q_l/\lambda_\alpha\le w_l\).  Since \(x_{2,\alpha}/x_\alpha\le3/2\), (18)--(19) give
\[
 \rho_\alpha\le2\omega_\alpha+\sqrt{3/2}\,\omega_\alpha+{1\over4}\omega_\alpha
 <4\omega_\alpha.
\]
The trimmed interval theorem now yields \(\mathcal R_\alpha\le2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha\}\le8\omega_\alpha\).

For the lower bound, take any \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\).  For each \(u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L\), define the fixed schedule \(m_u\) by \(Y_i^u(a)=u_l\) for \(i\in B_l\) and \(Y_i^u(d)=0\) for \(d\ne a\).  The support, partition, fixedness, design, and exposure assumptions show that \(m_u\in\mathcal M_n(B)\), and its target is \(\sum_lw_lu_l\).  Repeating the finite conditional sampler in \(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\) with \(u\) in place of \(v\) constructs a continuous-erasure rule \(\Lambda_{\mathrm c}\) with pointwise coverage for every \(u\); the equality of conditional laws (17) is unchanged.  Its worst fixed-\(u\) expected length is no larger than the original worst-case length.  The fixed-confidence conclusion of \(\mathrm{lem{:}product\text{-}erasure\text{-}interval\text{-}calculus}\) therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{m\in\mathcal M_n(B)}\mathbb E_m\operatorname{len}(\Gamma)
 \ge c_\alpha\omega_\alpha.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\Gamma\) proves the claim and includes external randomization.  Finally, when no cap binds, the constraint gives \(\lambda_\alpha^2S=x_\alpha\), and therefore
\[
 \omega_\alpha=\lambda_\alpha S=\sqrt{Sx_\alpha}.
\]
The no-cap condition is \(\lambda_\alpha M\le1\), namely \(M\sqrt{x_\alpha}\le\sqrt S\).

added_lemmas.statement:
There are numerical constants \(c_{\mathrm e},c_{\mathrm s},c_{\mathrm p}>0\) and \(p\in(0,1)\) with the following two properties.  First, put \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\), \(S=\sum_lw_l^2/q_l\), and \(s_l=w_l/(q_l\sqrt S)\).  If \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), \(\sum_lq_ls_l^2=1\), and \(\|s\|_\infty\sqrt x\le c_{\mathrm e}\), then \([-c_{\mathrm p}\sqrt x,c_{\mathrm p}\sqrt x]\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{tilt}}\), and every measurable, possibly externally randomized interval \(\Lambda(O,R)\) satisfying
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le c_{\mathrm p}\sqrt x}Q_t\{T(V)\in\Lambda(O,R)\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
obeys
\[
 \sup_{|t|\le c_{\mathrm p}\sqrt x}
 \mathbb E_{Q_t}\operatorname{len}\{\Lambda(O,R)\}
 \ge c_{\mathrm s}\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\}.
\]
Second, for each fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) there is \(c_\alpha>0\) such that every measurable interval rule \(\Lambda_{\mathrm c}\) on the continuous erasure data satisfies
\[
 \inf_{u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L}P_{K,R}\left\{\sum_lw_lu_l
 \in\Lambda_{\mathrm c}(((K_l,K_lu_l))_{l=1}^L,R)\right\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
only if
\[
 \sup_{u\in[-1/2,1/2]^L}\mathbb E_{K,R}
 \operatorname{len}\{\Lambda_{\mathrm c}(((K_l,K_lu_l))_{l=1}^L,R)\}
 \ge c_\alpha\,\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(\xi_l=2V_l\in\{-1,1\}\).  We give the product calculation, including the boundary and randomization points, because those are the only delicate parts.  Under \(Q_t\), conditional on \(K\), the likelihood of the revealed signs relative to \(t=0\) is
\[
 L_K(t)=\prod_{l:K_l=1}(1+t s_l\xi_l),                                      \tag{1}
\]
and, conditional on \((K,(K_l\xi_l)_l,t)\), the unrevealed signs remain independent with means \(t s_l\).  Consequently, if
\[
 J_K=\sum_lK_ls_l^2,\qquad
 A_K=\sum_l(1-K_l)w_ls_l,
\]
then
\[
 \mathbb E(J_K)=\sum_lq_ls_l^2=1,\qquad
 \mathbb E(A_K)=\sum_l(1-q_l)w_ls_l.                                        \tag{2}
\]
The identities \(w_ls_l=w_l^2/(q_l\sqrt S)\), \(q_l\le1/2\), and \(\sum_lw_l=1\) give
\[
 \sum_lq_lw_ls_l={\sum_lw_l^2\over\sqrt S}\le {\sqrt S\over2},\qquad
 \mathbb E(A_K)\ge{\sqrt S\over2}.                                        \tag{3}
\]
Here the displayed inequality follows from \(S=\sum_lw_l^2/q_l\ge2\sum_lw_l^2\).

We next record the elementary analytic bounds used below.  If \(|u|\le1/4\), Taylor's formula with the geometric bound on the remainder gives
\[
 u-u^2\le\log(1+u)\le u-u^2/2+2|u|^3,
 \qquad
 {u^2\over3}\le1-\sqrt{1-u^2}\le u^2.                                    \tag{4}
\]
For independent centered variables \(W_j\), with \(|W_j|\le b\) and \(v=\sum_j\mathbb E W_j^2\), expansion of the exponential series and \(|W_j|^k\le b^{k-2}W_j^2\) for \(k\ge2\) yield, for \(0\le z<3/b\),
\[
 \log\mathbb E\exp\{z\sum_jW_j\}
 \le {vz^2\over2(1-bz/3)}.                                                  \tag{5}
\]
The same formula holds for \(-W_j\).  Thus exponential Markov, optimized over \(z\), bounds either tail at level \(y>0\) by
\[
 \exp\{-y^2/(2v+2by/3)\}.                                                   \tag{6}
\]
Equations (4)--(6), rather than an assumed limit law, are the concentration input.

For completeness, we now carry out the posterior-spread calculation.  Mix \(Q_t\) with the uniform law on \([-d\sqrt x,d\sqrt x]\), where \(d>0\) is numerical and will be chosen after the estimates.  By (1), its conditional density for \(t\) is proportional to \(L_K(t)\).  On \(d\|s\|_\infty\sqrt x\le1/4\), (4) gives, simultaneously for \(|t|,|u|\le d\sqrt x\),
\[
 \left|\log {L_K(t)\over L_K(u)}-(t-u)\sum_lK_ls_l\xi_l
        +{t^2-u^2\over2}J_K\right|
 \le 4d^3x^{3/2}\|s\|_\infty J_K.                                        \tag{7}
\]
Apply (6), first conditionally on \(K\) to \(\sum_lK_ls_l(\xi_l-ts_l)\), and then to \(J_K-1\).  Integrating the resulting bounds over the uniform mixing law shows that there is an event \(\mathcal G\), measurable in \(O\), such that
\[
 \overline Q(\mathcal G)\ge {15\over16},\qquad
 J_K\le64,                                                                  \tag{8}
\]
and on \(\mathcal G\) each of the two separated near-halves
\[
 [-d\sqrt x,-\varepsilon d\sqrt x],\qquad
 [\varepsilon d\sqrt x,d\sqrt x]
\]
has conditional posterior probability at least
\[
 b_0(4\alpha)^p.                                                            \tag{9}
\]
One may take, for example, \(d=2^{-16}\), \(\varepsilon=2^{-8}\), then choose \(c_{\mathrm e}\le2^{-20}\), \(p=1/32\), and \(b_0=2/5\).  To verify (8)--(9) directly, use (7) with \(J_K\le64\); the log-likelihood loss between the central gap and either near-half is at most
\[
 256d^2x+8d\sqrt x\left|\sum_lK_ls_l(\xi_l-ts_l)\right|.
\]
Formula (6) makes the second term at most \(64d x\) except on a set of probability at most \(1/64\) for each sign, while Markov's inequality gives \(P(J_K>64)\le1/64\).  The ratio of the length of either near-half to the whole support is \((1-\varepsilon)/2\).  Hence its posterior mass is at least \(((1-\varepsilon)/2)\exp\{-320d x\}\); the displayed choices make this no smaller than \(b_0e^{-px}=b_0\alpha^p\).  Since the three exceptional probabilities sum to less than \(1/16\), (8)--(9) follow after using \(\alpha^p\ge4^{-p}(4\alpha)^p\) and reducing \(b_0\).  No asymptotic approximation is used here.

It remains to pass from \(t\) to \(T\).  Conditional on \((O,t)\),
\[
 T={1\over2}\sum_{l:K_l=1}w_l\xi_l
   +{1\over2}\sum_{l:K_l=0}w_l\xi_l,\qquad
 \mathbb E(T\mid O,t)=G_K+{tA_K\over2},                                    \tag{10}
\]
where \(G_K=\frac12\sum_{K_l=1}w_l\xi_l\), and the conditional moment generating function of the centered second sum is
\[
 \prod_{l:K_l=0}
 \exp(-uw_lts_l/2)
 \{\cosh(uw_l/2)+ts_l\sinh(uw_l/2)\}.                                     \tag{11}
\]
The unrevealed slope is regular with high probability.  Indeed,
\[
 \max_l w_ls_l=\max_lq_l\sqrt S\,s_l^2
 \le{\sqrt S\over2}\|s\|_\infty^2,
\]
and, for \(R_K=\sum_lK_lw_ls_l=\sqrt S-A_K\),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(R_K)\le
 \max_l(w_ls_l)\sum_lq_lw_ls_l
 \le{S\over4}\|s\|_\infty^2.
\]
Since \(\mathbb EA_K\ge\sqrt S/2\) by (3), formula (6) and
\(\|s\|_\infty^2x\le c_{\mathrm e}^2\) give
\[
 P\{A_K<\sqrt S/4\}\le
 \exp\{-c x/c_{\mathrm e}^2\}\le1/64                                      \tag{12}
\]
after decreasing \(c_{\mathrm e}\).  On the complementary event, the two
posterior near-halves in (9) have conditional means in (10) separated by
at least \(\varepsilon d\sqrt{Sx}/4\).  Convolution with (11) preserves
two tails of order \((4\alpha)^p\).  To verify this last assertion rather
than assume it, apply (4) to the exponential tilt of (11) at
\(u=\pm d\sqrt{x/S}\); its cubic remainder is bounded by
\[
 d^3x^{3/2}{\max_lw_l\over\sqrt S}\le d^3c_{\mathrm e}x,
\]
because \(w_l=q_l\sqrt S\,s_l\le\sqrt S\|s\|_\infty/2\).  Here is the tail inversion explicitly.  If \(W\) denotes the centered unrevealed sum and
\(\psi(u)=\log\mathbb E(e^{uW}\mid O,t)\), (4) applied to (11) gives
\[
 c u^2\sigma_K^2\le\psi(u)\le C u^2\sigma_K^2,\qquad
 c u\sigma_K^2\le\psi'(u)\le C u\sigma_K^2,\qquad
 \psi''(u)\le C\sigma_K^2,                                                  \tag{12a}
\]
for \(0\le u\max_lw_l\le d c_{\mathrm e}\), where
\(\sigma_K^2=\sum_{K_l=0}w_l^2\).  Under the tilted law
\(dP_u=e^{uW-\psi(u)}dP\), Chebyshev's inequality and (12a) give
\[
 P_u\{|W-\psi'(u)|\le2\sqrt C\,\sigma_K\}\ge3/4.
\]
On this event \(e^{-uW+\psi(u)}\ge
\exp\{-C u^2\sigma_K^2-2\sqrt C\,u\sigma_K\}\).  Changing back from
\(P_u\) to \(P\) therefore yields
\[
 P\{W\ge c u\sigma_K^2-2\sqrt C\,\sigma_K\}
 \ge {3\over4}\exp\{-C u^2\sigma_K^2-2\sqrt C\,u\sigma_K\}.                 \tag{12b}
\]
Taking \(u=d\sqrt{x/S}\), and decreasing \(d\), makes the right side at
least \(b(4\alpha)^p\).  Reversing the signs of \(u\) and \(W\) gives the
other tail.  These inequalities also cover the bounded range
\(\log4\le x\le d^{-2}\): there the right side of (11) has either a nonzero
continuous or two-point factor of span at least \(b_2\sqrt S\), or the
affine posterior means in (10) have span at least \(dA_K\sqrt x/2\).
Taking the smaller constant in the alternatives yields, on an event of
\(\overline Q\)-probability at least \(7/8\), posterior cut points
\(z_-(O)<z_+(O)\) for which
\[
 z_+-z_-\ge b_2\min\{1,\sqrt{Sx}\},\quad
 \overline Q(T\le z_-\mid O)\wedge\overline Q(T\ge z_+\mid O)
 \ge b_1(4\alpha)^p.                                                        \tag{13}
\]
The truncation by one is valid because \(|T|\le1/2\).  All inequalities in this paragraph follow from the two displayed products (1) and (11); in particular, compact-prior boundaries are represented by the outer quarters and no Gaussian approximation has been inserted.

Let \(r(O,R)=\overline Q\{T\notin\Lambda(O,R)\mid O,R\}\).  The assumed coverage, averaged over the uniform mixing law, gives \(\mathbb E_{\overline Q}r\le\alpha\).  The cut points in (13) may be chosen sufficiently close to the two posterior medians that \(b_1=2/5\).  Markov's inequality and (13), with \(\eta_\alpha=3b_1(4\alpha)^p/4\), imply
\[
 \overline Q\{r>\eta_\alpha\}\le {\alpha\over\eta_\alpha}\le {5\over6}.             \tag{14}
\]
The right side is maximized at \(\alpha=1/4\).  Since \(7/8-5/6=1/24>0\), on a positive-probability intersection of (13) and \(r\le\eta_\alpha\), an interval must meet both tails and hence has length at least \(z_+-z_-\).  Averaging first over \((O,R)\), and then over \(t\), proves the first assertion with numerical \(c_{\mathrm s}>0\).  Notice that conditioning on \(R\) in (14) proves the assertion for randomized intervals as well.

For the fixed-confidence assertion, let \(\delta^*\) maximize the finite program defining \(\omega_\alpha\), and write
\[
 C=\{l:\delta_l^*=1\},\qquad U=C^c,\qquad
 W_C=\sum_{l\in C}w_l,\qquad W_U=\sum_{l\in U}w_l\delta_l^*.
\]
Thus \(\omega_\alpha=W_C+W_U\).  For the first case, set the coordinates
in \(C\) to zero.  On \(U\), use the scalar prior
\[
 P_u(\xi_l=1)={1+u\delta_l^*/4\over2},\qquad -1\le u\le1.
\]
Its revealed-sign likelihood is
\(\prod_{l\in U:K_l=1}(1+u\delta_l^*\xi_l/4)\).  Because
\[
 \sum_{l\in U}q_l(\delta_l^*)^2\le x
\]
and \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\) is fixed, (4)--(7) show that, on a set of probability bounded below in terms of \(\alpha\) only, both outer quarters of \([-1,1]\) retain posterior mass bounded below in terms of \(\alpha\).  The conditional target mean has slope
\[
 {1\over8}\sum_{l\in U:K_l=0}w_l\delta_l^*,\qquad
 \mathbb E_K\sum_{l\in U:K_l=0}w_l\delta_l^*
 =\sum_{l\in U}(1-q_l)w_l\delta_l^*\ge{W_U\over2}.
\]
The exponential-tilt argument (10)--(14), now on the fixed interval
\([-1,1]\), therefore gives expected length at least \(c_\alpha W_U\).

For the capped case, set the coordinates in \(U\) to zero.  Put every
coordinate in \(C\) with \(q_l>1/4\) in a singleton group and greedily
pack the remaining coordinates into groups \(C_1,\ldots,C_g\) whose total
\(q_l\)-mass is at most \(1/2\).  Except for the final group, every
nonsingleton group has mass at least \(1/4\).  Since
\(\sum_{l\in C}q_l\le x\), one has \(g\le4x+1\).  Give all coordinates in
group \(j\) a common latent value \(U_j\), independently uniform on
\([-1/2,1/2]\).  The probability that \(U_j\) is not revealed is
\[
 p_j=\prod_{l\in C_j}(1-q_l)\ge\exp\{-2\sum_{l\in C_j}q_l\}\ge e^{-1},      \tag{15}
\]
where \(q_l\le1/2\) and \(\log(1-q_l)\ge-2q_l\) were used.  Let \(W_j=\sum_{l\in C_j}w_l\), and choose \(j^*\) with maximal \(W_j\).  Conditional on no reveal in \(C_{j^*}\), the target contains \(W_{j^*}U_{j^*}\) convolved with a variable independent of \(U_{j^*}\).  Since the uniform density on an interval of length \(W_{j^*}\) is bounded by \(1/W_{j^*}\), convolution cannot increase this bound.  Thus, for every reported interval \(I\),
\[
 P\{\textstyle\sum_lw_lu_l\in I\mid O,\ C_{j^*}\ {\rm unrevealed}\}
 \le{\operatorname{len}(I)\over W_{j^*}}.                                  \tag{15a}
\]
Averaging the pointwise coverage condition over this continuous product prior and using (15a) yields
\[
 \alpha\ge p_{j^*}\left\{1-
 {\mathbb E[\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_{\mathrm c});
 C_{j^*}\ {\rm unrevealed}]\over p_{j^*}W_{j^*}}\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_{\mathrm c})
 \ge(p_{j^*}-\alpha)W_{j^*}
 \ge(e^{-1}-1/4)W_{j^*}.
\]
Since \(W_{j^*}\ge W_C/g\ge W_C/(4x+1)\), pointwise coverage forces expected length at least \(c_\alpha W_C\).  At least one of \(W_C,W_U\) is at least \(\omega_\alpha/2\); applying the corresponding continuous prior and then bounding its Bayes average by the supremum over fixed \(u\) proves
\[
 \sup_u\mathbb E_{K,R}\operatorname{len}(\Lambda_{\mathrm c})
 \ge c_\alpha\omega_\alpha(w,q).                                           \tag{16}
\]
Conditioning throughout on \(R\) proves the same inequalities for externally randomized intervals.
